title: The race around the world
hookLine: Ganesha vs Kartikeya: one circles the earth, one circles his parents; why Hindus honor parents like gods
carry: circle your parents like a temple
tomorrow: so why is one of Ganesha's tusks snapped short?

cards: Your phone counts every step you take. It has no idea which ones mattered. Here's a race about that.

Two brothers: Kartikeya, the warrior, fast and bright on his peacock, and Ganesha, round and patient on his mouse. Their parents, Shiva and Parvati, set a contest: whoever goes around the whole world first, wins.
Kartikeya is gone before the sentence ends, over mountains, over oceans. Ganesha looks at his mouse. The mouse looks at Ganesha.
Then Ganesha walks to his mother and father and, slowly, walks one circle around them. He bows. I'm done, he says.

teach.b: Kartikeya lands, out of breath, to find his brother already declared the winner.
In the Shiva Purana, Ganesha explains: the scriptures say that walking around your parents with devotion is the same as walking around the earth.
That walk has a name, pradakshina: circling something holy, keeping it on your right. Hindus do it around temple shrines, sacred trees, and the fire at a wedding.
It's the body saying: this is the center, and I move around it. And Ganesha does it around his mother and father. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, parents are honored almost like gods.

teach.h: MATRU DEVO BHAVA: YOUR MOTHER AS GOD.
teach.b: An old line children learn says it plainly: matru devo bhava, pitru devo bhava. Let your mother be God to you; let your father be God to you.
It's why many Hindu kids bow and touch their parents' and grandparents' feet, and get a blessing back.

The tellings differ on the prize: in the Shiva Purana it's who marries first; in South India it's a fruit of wisdom, and Kartikeya, called Murugan there, leaves for the hill of Palani, where pilgrims still climb to his temple.

teach.h: CIRCLE YOUR PARENTS LIKE A TEMPLE.
teach.b: He really went around the world. Ganesha just knew where his world was.

how: Hindus walk pradakshina, a clockwise circle keeping the holy on their right, around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire. Many children greet parents and elders by bowing and touching their feet, and receive a blessing; this story is often told to explain why parents are honored.

s: Ganesha cheated his brother out of the prize
his walk is pradakshina, the same circling Hindus do at temples, and in the Shiva Purana he cites scripture for it.
every telling says the prize was a fruit
in the Shiva Purana it's who marries first; the fruit version is told in South India.
Ganesha's circle shows parents honored almost like gods
matru devo bhava, pitru devo bhava: let your mother, and your father, be God to you.

games.q: at a Hindu wedding, your friend sees the bride bend and touch her grandmother's feet, and asks why. what would Ganesha's race tell her?
o: parents and elders are honored almost like gods. Ganesha circled his as his whole world.
it's an old rule about who outranks whom in the family.
it's mostly for the wedding photos.
games.why: matru devo bhava: let your mother be God to you. Ganesha walked pradakshina around his parents; touching an elder's feet is the same honor, and a blessing comes back.

practice: Stand up, if you can, and pick a center: a photo of your parents or grandparents, or whoever raised you, or a chair where you picture them. Walk slowly around it, keeping it on your right, one step for each breath.

With each circle, name one thing they gave you. Then stop and bow, the way many Hindus do at a shrine or at an elder's feet. If standing isn't possible, trace a slow circle with one finger around their names.
If those relationships are hard, choose an elder who has been a blessing to you.

wordCard.voice: Pradakshina: the circle walked around something holy, keeping it on your right. One brother circled the earth. The other circled his parents.

orig.note: Sanskrit: circling toward the right, walking around something holy.

carryVoice: Something to keep from the race: circle your parents like a temple. Ganesha's whole world was a few steps away. Until tomorrow.
